title: Variables and Data Types
description: C's basic types (char, int, float, double, void), signed/unsigned, short/long, and constants.
objectives: Declare variables of C's basic types
Understand signed vs. unsigned and short/long modifiers

content.heading: Basic Types
content.body: C's basic types are char (a single byte, typically an 8-bit character/small integer), int (the default integer type, typically 32-bit on modern systems, though C only guarantees a minimum range, not an exact size), float (32-bit single-precision floating point), double (64-bit double-precision floating point, the default for decimal literals), and void (meaning 'no type' — used for a function returning nothing, or a generic pointer type). Every variable must be declared with an explicit type before use, and C (unlike Python) does not auto-initialize local variables — an uninitialized local variable holds whatever indeterminate bits happened to be in that memory already.

content.heading: Signed/Unsigned, Short/Long, and Constants
content.body:
Integer types can be modified with signed (the default; can represent negative values) or unsigned (only non-negative values, doubling the positive range for the same number of bits by giving up the sign) — unsigned int max_count; is common for values that logically can never be negative, like a count or size. short and long adjust an integer type's size: short int (often 16-bit) and long int / long long int (at least 32-bit and 64-bit respectively) for a smaller or larger range than plain int.

Constants are declared two ways: const int MAX = 100; (a properly typed, compiler-checked constant, enforced at the language level — reassignment is a compile error) or #define MAX 100 (a preprocessor macro — a pure textual substitution performed before compilation even starts, with no type checking at all). Modern C style generally favors const for typed constants, reserving #define for cases that genuinely need textual substitution or conditional compilation.

content.explanation: MAX_USERS is a properly typed, compiler-enforced constant; VERSION is a preprocessor macro, substituted textually before compilation. Each printf format specifier matches its corresponding argument's type.

keyPoints: C's basic types: char, int, float, double, void, each with implementation-defined (but minimum-guaranteed) sizes
unsigned trades the ability to represent negatives for a larger positive range
short/long adjust an integer type's size relative to plain int
const declares a typed, compiler-enforced constant; #define performs untyped textual substitution
commonMistakes: Reading an uninitialized local variable, getting indeterminate garbage rather than a predictable default
Assigning a negative value to an unsigned variable, silently wrapping to a very large positive number
Assuming int is always exactly 32 bits on every platform (C only guarantees a minimum range)
